We investigate the generation of multipartite genuine entanglement among three otherwise uncorrelated and independent systems through genuine quantum interactions between a single one of those systems and the others. A key finding is that if the atom-photon interaction occurs at a specific interaction strength, two uncorrelated atoms interacting via one photon will produce a W state; subsequently, utilizing this state as an input for a second, identically tuned interaction generates genuine multipartite entanglement among three atoms. We further demonstrate that if this sequence of interactions is repeated $n$ times, two initial uncorrelated atoms can yield a target state of genuine multipartite entanglement involving $n+1$ atoms. It is also established that if the photons are generated at the same frequency as the atoms, the resulting state between two photons is a two-mode squeezed state. If these interactions occur at a different frequency, the two-mode squeezed state transforms into a two-mode squeezed vacuum state.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector, situated within LHC's ATLAS and ALICE companions, serves as the primary instrument dedicated to comprehensively analyzing and characterizing the outcomes of high-energy proton-proton collisions. As a critical component of this system, the Silicon Pixel Detector is optimized for the high luminosity conditions anticipated at the Large Hadron Collider's subsequent collision runs, known as the HL-LHC. This text provides an overview of the engineering design, operational principles, and performance metrics of the Silicon Pixel Detector, detailing its ability to track leptons (electrons and muons), identify photons by reconstructing their conversion tracks, and manage the challenging signatures arising from high-mass, long-lived particle decays. Furthermore, the document examines the detector's specialized capacity to enhance the mass resolution of J/psi and Upsilon states, as well as its general application in identifying and analyzing exotic hadrons.

We introduce a new inversion formula for the Euclidean Lattice Lightray K\"all\'en-Lehmann spectral density, $\rho_\text{LK}(s)$, which expresses it as an integral involving only a single (unsubtracted) propagator. Although the formula is derived for a generic Euclidean lattice theory with a symmetric, positive-definite kernel, its application in lattice QCD allows $\rho_\\text{LK}(s)$ to be determined directly from standard simulations. By projecting onto specific polynomial bases, one obtains the irreducible Hadron plus continuum cuts, offering a direct method to extract hadron masses and matrix elements from first principles. Furthermore, the formalism is extended to incorporate the impact of blocking procedures on the lattice.

Emotional monitoring on platforms like Twitter is increasingly vital for a wide range of applications, necessitating a robust method for analyzing public sentiment expressed on the service. This study proposes a new deep learning architecture designed to detect sentiments within Twitter data, leveraging an innovative information fusion strategy that integrates both visual and textual content from users' posts. Empirical analyses of the proposed model's performance across two distinct datasets demonstrate its superior accuracy compared to existing baselines, while a comprehensive examination of the model's hyperparameters provides further insights into its optimal configuration.

Non-equilibrium dynamics of strongly interacting theories can be investigated through holography by analyzing the event horizon's dynamics. In this study, we examine the dynamics of a four-dimensional anti-de Sitter (AdS) black hole within strongly coupled, large-$N_c$ quantum chromodynamics (QCD). We derive an effective surface tension acting on the black hole's horizon and demonstrate that it correlates inversely with the shadow's radius. Furthermore, we derive effective viscosities for radial and transverse directions; unlike the surface tension, these viscosities increase as the shadow's radius decreases. By employing dynamic shadow analysis, we can identify critical points in non-equilibrium phase transitions and determine the direction of the transition by comparing radial and transverse shadow radii. Finally, we observe that in the spinodal region, the shadow's ellipticity reaches its maximum value.

Reconstructing quantum states of infinite-dimensional spaces, such as those of light, is a fundamental yet challenging endeavor in quantum mechanics. Two primary approaches exist for this task: direct methods, which rely on experimentally accessible quantities like expectation values of orthogonal polynomials, and indirect methods, which utilize machine learning to map raw experimental data to quantum states. This study presents a novel, direct reconstruction technique applied to a one-dimensional mode of light (with similar applicability to continuous variable systems in higher-dimensional spaces). Specifically, this method extracts a Wigner function from the tomographic profile obtained via standard tomography. While the example focuses on states with a dominant coherent character, the approach is expected to function for any state within such subspaces. Distinguishing itself from existing algorithms, this procedure demands no prior knowledge of the spectral properties of the system's annihilation operator nor does it involve iterative optimization. Instead, it calculates the values of the density matrix elements in the Fock basis by performing specific integrations over the optical tomogram.

Open-ended dialogue models have proven to be a valuable asset in human-computer interaction, yet introducing traits like persona or safety constraints often leads to sample rejection rates. To improve learning in this specific context, we introduce a new framework grounded in the Fundamental Frequency Framework (F3), which emphasizes flexibility, faithfulness, and fidelity. Our proposed approach, Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning with Overlapping Networks (MTRLON), utilizes shared neural components to generate responses while simultaneously mastering multiple auxiliary tasks. By learning to balance these tasks through a weighted combination strategy, the system ensures that critical constraints, such as safety guidelines and user-defined personas, are consistently integrated into generated outputs. Experimental results across three distinct datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in upholding these specified features.

Farmers are increasingly utilizing statistical approaches to assess the effectiveness of pesticides by analyzing treatment outcomes against historical data. However, evaluating efficacy requires accounting for temporal and spatial field variability, which often necessitates dividing fields into subunits, known as strips. This study examines various design and analysis strategies for experiments conducted within agricultural field strips. We contrast common practices, such as treating the entire field as a single experimental unit, with more rigorous methods like randomized complete block designs (RCBD) employing the strip as a blocking factor. Furthermore, we evaluate the impact of analyzing data at the individual plant level versus the strip-averaged plant level. Our findings indicate that the RCBD combined with an analysis of mean strip values offers the most robust analytical framework. This approach yields more reliable $p$-values and confidence intervals compared to other methods, effectively enhancing both statistical power and precision.

"6G" is expected to be the next generation of mobile networks, and 6G-enabled 360-degree video streaming is a key application that can significantly improve virtual tourism by offering more immersive experiences. To meet the high data rates required for this technology, 6G relies on intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) to reflect signals and create connectivity. This study introduces an efficient reflection coefficient optimization method for 6G 360-degree video streaming assisted by IRS. Unlike traditional approaches that use a single reflection pattern for all users, the proposed technique employs user-specific configurations to optimize video quality. Furthermore, it utilizes a learning-based algorithm to optimize video streaming under various channel conditions using a Q-learning framework. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing baselines in performance.

"Matrix product operator methods are commonly employed to simulate both equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium systems, provided that the time evolution scale or inverse temperature allows for a sufficiently low bond dimension. However, these techniques have lacked support for strongly interacting many-body topological models. In response, we introduce Matrix Product Ground States parameterized by thermal and inverse temperature, designed to represent either equilibrium eigenstates belonging specific topological sectors or excited states with exact topological order. Furthermore, by implementing the Thomas-Fermi variational approach within our specific framework, we derive efficient methods for locating highly excited, globally entangled topologically ordered states. As a demonstration of its efficacy, we show that for the 4-body toric code and the 5-body magic square model on a ring, this approach successfully generates accurate excited states even in large systems where traditional methods typically struggle.

This research examines the decoupling theory for a broad class of $C^4$ surfaces in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that possess non-vanishing Gaussian and at least one non-zero principal curvature. These surfaces include graphs of functions $f:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ where the Hessian matrix of $f$ has at least one non-zero eigenvalue with $\|D^2f\|_\infty \leq 1$ and all its derivatives are uniformly bounded. The paper demonstrates that these surfaces admit a decoupling constant $\delta(\epsilon)$ for any $\delta > 0$ such that $\epsilon \leq 1$. Furthermore, the constants involved are demonstrated to be stable under $\mathitL^\infty$-small perturbations of both the surface definition and the target set.

This paper establishes a precise anisotropic $L^p$ Minkowski inequality that incorporates total $L^p$ anisotropic mean curvature and anisotropic $p$-capacity, applicable to any bounded domains with smooth boundaries in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Derived as consequences are inequalities relating anisotropic $L^p$ mean curvature with anisotropic surface area, as well as various sharp forms of the anisotropic isoperimetric and ALM inequalities. The core approach relies on demonstrating a Frobenius-complete vector field within an anisotropic setting. Additionally, we provide characterizations of the equality cases within our primary result.

The MICROSCOPE mission, launched in April 2016 by the French Space Agency (CNES), aims to conduct high-precision tests of the Weak Equivalence Principle (WEP). This principle asserts that all particles share identical gravitational accelerations regardless of their composition. The WEP serves as a cornerstone of General Relativity; consequently, observing its violation would constitute a significant finding in fundamental physics. Nanometer-scale rare-earth-transition metal (RE-TM) alloys are highly promising for ultrafast magnetophotonic applications due to their strong light-matter interactions and exceptionally rapid all-optical switching speeds. Nevertheless, achieving optical resonance matching with these materials remains a significant challenge that limits their full potential. To overcome this limitation, we propose a hybrid structure combining nanoscale RE-TM alloys with plasmonic nanoantenna arrays. This configuration leverages the lightweight properties of the RE-TM layer alongside the enhanced light-matter coupling capabilities of the surrounding antennas. This design yields a magnetic dipolar far-field interaction exhibiting a giant magneto-optical effect characterized by a 3000 cm$^{-1}$ Kerr field strength and a distinct 200 meV Kerr detuning from optical resonance. Furthermore, the magnitude of both the Kerr field and detuning is tunable via the Kerr shift mechanism, enabling a dynamic change in Kerr detuning of approximately 200 meV. Consequently, this architecture establishes a robust foundation for developing high-performance magnetophotonic devices, including ultrafast all-optical Kerr solitons.

Knowledge distillation serves as a crucial technique for expediting deep neural networks, functioning by having a smaller "student" model replicate the behaviors of larger "teacher" networks. A significant challenge lies in the fact that students often fail to adequately capture the intricate input-output mappings of their instructors. This study demonstrates that the stochastic nature of mini-batch training is instrumental in facilitating this knowledge transfer. Leveraging this finding, we propose a novel approach wherein the student is trained on mini-batches, while the teacher is reconfigured to stochotically select data points drawn from the same batch according to a soft probability distribution. Empirical results indicate substantial performance enhancements over conventional distillation methods utilizing full-batch teaching and standard loss functions, particularly when a significantly less capacity student learns from a high-capacity teacher. These improvements are observed across various architectures, including ResNets, VGGs, and Vision Transformers.

Constructing the submodule lattice $L(M)$ for an arbitrary module $M$ is a fundamental challenge in computational algebraic geometry and algebraic programming. The proposed approach relies on the concept of $\lambda$-join irreducible submodules, which generalizes the $H$-form used previously. By utilizing this generalized structure, the algorithm efficiently handles cases where $M$ is large but the lattice $L(M)$ is relatively compact. For efficiency, the user-provided module structure map need only be defined on a basis of the algebra's vector space space, without requiring an explicit dual map.

In a graph $G=(V,E)$, a set $S \subseteq V$ qualifies as a strong geodetic set if there exists $\lambda_v > 0$ for each $v \in V$ such that the shortest path from any node $u$ to any set element satisfies $d(u,S)=\lambda_v$ along the unique ray $(v_t)_{t \ge 0}$ originating at $u$ and passing through $v$. The associated weighted set, defined by pairs $(S, \lambda)$, minimizes the total weight $\sum_{v \in V} \lambda_v$ when $\lambda$ is optimal. This paper demonstrates that deciding whether a graph contains a strong geodetic set is computationally NP-complete, whereas determining graphs where a strong geodetic set exists can be resolved in polynomial time. Furthermore, for graphs admitting such a set, explicit formulas are derived for both the minimum weight sum $\sum \lambda_v$ and the corresponding weighting scheme $\lambda$.

Imitation learning typically relies on access to optimal, task-specific trajectories; however, acquiring such high-quality data is often difficult. Conversely, collecting vast quantities of suboptimal or task-agnostic trajectories is relatively straightforward. This paper explores the potential of utilizing these subpar or generic trajectories to enhance imitation learning. We demonstrate that by integrating reinforcement learning with graph neural networks to reconstruct missing segments from trajectories containing gaps, it becomes possible to transform these incomplete paths into superior, optimized trajectories. Experimental results indicate that this approach yields a significant improvement over traditional imitation learning methods that depend solely on perfect trajectories.

Imitation learning primarily enhances reinforcement learning efficiency by utilizing expert demonstrations. However, acquiring such demonstrations from perfect experts is often impractical. To address this gap, this paper proposes a novel approach that utilizes suboptimal trajectories generated by an actor-critic agent to facilitate both the reinforcement learning process and the rapid generation of near-optimal demonstrations. This method operates within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework where the goal is to master multiple distinct but related tasks. The proposed solution enables an agent to learn Task 1 through trajectories containing near-optimal solutions for Task 2, thereby accelerating learning across both. Theoretical analysis confirms that both the agent and the demonstration generator achieve linear convergence rates. Extensive experiments across various testbeds validate these findings and demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in practice.

In image recognition, edges play a fundamental role as they delineate object boundaries and define shapes. Although modern deep learning architectures have significantly enhanced recognition accuracy across various domains, their utility in medical contexts remains constrained by the difficulty of obtaining large-scale annotated datasets. To mitigate this challenge, this paper introduces a novel data augmentation technique specifically designed to improve the segmentation of medical structures using deep learning. The proposed method employs an edge-preserving algorithm to generate multiple data variations for each original image. These enhanced datasets are then utilized to train a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) segmentation model. The approach was validated on the ISBI 2015 Micro-CT 3D Mastocytoma Segmentation Challenge, demonstrating significant performance gains over standard approaches using only original images. Furthermore, the method was assessed on a secondary, real-world Mastocytoma case, yielding consistent and promising results.

MongoDB is a widely adopted, highly available, horizontally scalable, document-oriented database. It offers transaction support that varies by deployment: ACID-compliant transactions on replicasets and sharded collections (with key-based range routing), as well as eventual consistency guarantees on single-document operations for single instances. This paper presents the first formal analysis of atomicity and consistency in MongoDB across all its deployment models. We develop a comprehensive execution model for these deployments and introduce a new atomicity oracle to track committed transactions. Our analysis demonstrates that atomicity guarantees on shards aligns with the Three-Phase Commit (2PC) protocol, whereas single-instance behavior mirrors a 2PC-like approach using per-collection write locks. Furthermore, we formalize MongoDB's consistency options for documents, comparing them against established consistency models to offer the most detailed atomic and consistency specifications available for the system to date.

We introduce a method for Few-Shot Continuous Learning (FCCL) that simulates human executive function by dynamically allocating computational resources to tasks of varying difficulty. In this approach, harder tasks receive more resources, while easier ones receive fewer, enabling efficient handling of task sequences without explicit prior knowledge of task order or number. Furthermore, we employ a state-of-the-art generative adversarial network (GAN) to create synthetic lesions tailored to underrepresented demographic groups, thereby offering insights into potential dataset biases and informing the refinement of training materials for medical imaging algorithms.

Finally, the proposed model averaging framework shows robustness when utilizing models trained on both laboratory and live datasets.

We have assembled a high-resolution, deep, and spatially resolved near-infrared tidal feature sample specifically targeting massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) located at intermediate distances ($\sim$10–50 kpc). Utilizing the Hubble Space Telescope's WFC3/IR instrument, this coherent dataset covers a total area of $0.64\, \mathrm{deg}^2$ and includes 54 ETGs situated between heliocentric distances of $10^4$ and $40^4$ parsecs. The spatially resolved flux analysis reveals that roughly 50\% of extremely massive ETGs ($M_{\mathrm{ETG}} > 10^{11}\, \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$) display prominent tidal structures ($f_{\mathrm{TID}} > 1\%$). Furthermore, the occurrence rate of these features scales positively with host galaxy mass, following the relation $n_{\mathrm{TID}} \propto M_{\mathrm{ETG}}^{0.5}$. By combining this observed tidal fraction with the established ETG luminosity function, we determine the space density of such events to be $n_{\mathrm{TID}} \approx 10^{-5}\, \mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, specifically for systems where $f_{\mathrm{TID}} > 1\%$ and $M_{\mathrm{ET

The expansion of higher education serves as a crucial catalyst for intergenerational mobility, yet the specific mechanisms by which this occurs remain largely unexamined. This paper formulates and tests a theoretical framework designed to evaluate competing hypotheses regarding such mobility. Empirical analysis relies on data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) covering 1984 to 2010, which includes detailed parental occupational histories. The study finds robust support for the "supply-side hypothesis," which posits that mobility is driven by individual decisions to invest in education, rather than by direct government subsidies. Furthermore, the results indicate that the likelihood of obtaining a university degree is significantly influenced by a parent's non-manual status, particularly when that status is held at an advanced hierarchical level.

Chirped pulse amplification (CPA) and associated nonlinear optical (NLO) systems have become fundamental technologies across the photonics field, with widespread applications in spectroscopy, medical diagnostics, industrial manufacturing, and microscopic imaging. To meet the rising demand for compactness, versatility, and affordability, we present a fiber-based CPA setup integrated with an all-NLO spectral broadening scheme. This integrated fiber-CAP and NLO system offers a range of functionalities, including variable pulse energy, tunable duration, and broad spectral coverage.

In 2016, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) successfully carried out a pilot study on emittance scanning using single electron bunches, utilizing the beam instrumentation and controls systems. This paper outlines the strategy for developing the scanning technique over a multi-year period, beginning with the initial proof-of-concept in 2017 and progressing through stages with two bunch bunches and ultimately independent bunches by 2020. This incremental approach marks a novel application of LHC instrumentation, aiming to enhance bunch-by-bunch luminosity monitoring and refine the understanding of longitudinal and transverse beam-beam interactions.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. To mitigate these effects, we introduce two novel corruption strategies: **Rational Adversarial** and **Irrational Adversarial** attacks. In the rational model, the agent acts selfishly to maximize the distance from the global optimum while minimizing communication expenditure; conversely, the irrational agent acts as an omniscient, omnipresent entity that continuously drives the system off-manifold regardless of the network state. Correspondingly, this paper proposes **Rational Adversarial Resilient Optimization (RAO)** and **Irrational Adversarial Resilient Optimization (IAO)** algorithms. Both methods ensure that the connected, lossy, multi-agent system achieves a desired level of sub-optimality with high bandwidth efficiency. Notably, the IAO algorithm guarantees convergence to a small neighborhood of the global optimal solution under the influence of irrational attacks, operating with communication complexity that scales linearly with the square root of the total node count ($\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$).

Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) serves as a primary method for determining the age and composition of the universe. Although current technology allows for observations at angular scales down to approximately one arcminute ($1'$), the goal is to achieve resolution as fine as ten arcseconds ($10''$). This enhancement is critical for mapping primordial inflation and detecting cosmic strings, yet it necessitates precise measurements of the millisecond-polarized CMB signal. Such precision demands the use of dielectric lenses with an effective refractive index near 2.8 and exceptional structural accuracy. However, at these millisecond dimensions, polarization effects induced by the lensing material itself become significant. We demonstrate that, despite these challenges, the required precision is achievable by employing a two-layer design composed of polyethylene and Teflon. This configuration reduces residual polarization artifacts to levels below $10^{-5}$, ensuring the integrity of future high-resolution CMB studies.

Word reordering represents a fundamental natural language generation challenge, one where recent experiments indicate modern pre-trained language models (PLMs) often underperform compared to classical rule-based or statistical approaches. In this study, we evaluate several semi-supervised learning strategies to adapt the powerful BART model for the task of word ordering. Utilizing the extensive world knowledge embedded within large training corpora, BART proves particularly effective when applied to word ordering given only a small set of labeled training data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the benefits derived from leveraging vast training data diminish significantly once only a modest amount is provided, suggesting that the primary improvements stem from the model's ability to effectively utilize comprehensive linguistic and semantic knowledge through a semi-supervised framework.

The rapid advancement of deepfake generation technologies poses a significant threat to social security, necessitating the development of more robust detection algorithms. Current deepfake识别 methods primarily rely on extracting spatial features, often overlooking the critical role of frequency-domain features. This study introduces a novel cross-domain architecture that integrates frequency and spatial information to enhance deepfake detection. Specifically, we propose a Frequency Domain Discriminator (FDD) designed to leverage frequency features as an auxiliary classification task, alongside a traditional spatial domain discriminator. To facilitate the effective fusion of these cross-modal features, a Bidirectional Transfer Network (BTDN) is introduced; it enables the flow of information in both directions, with the primary generation of the image-like image from learned frequency representations. Experimental results indicate that this proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across four major deepfake datasets.

Most prior research on the analytical analysis of LDPC code performance over a binary erasure channel (BEC) presumes that degree distributions at encoder and decoder nodes follow independent choices, thereby ignoring degree-degree correlations. This assumption holds for randomly constructed code graphs but fails for those generated via message-passing (MP) learning techniques, which often yield structures with significant correlations. Consequently, traditional analytical methods are inadequate for assessing the performance of learned graphs, especially when examining erasure eroders (BECs) that exhibit correlation-based erasure probabilities. This paper introduces an analytical framework for general check-and-variable degree-degree correlated graphs operating over BECs that incorporate such correlation-based erasure mechanisms. We outline a set of message-passing equations tailored to these correlated graphs and verify the approach using a specific variable and check graph topology with linear degree-degree correlations, applying it to decode a corresponding linear-degree-correlation LDPC code. The proposed method is demonstrated to accurately predict the performance of related learning-based graphs under correlated erasure conditions.

While quantum key distribution (QKD) has matured into a commercially viable technology for secure communications, its implementation relies on optical components that deviate from theoretical ideals. These imperfections create side-channel vulnerabilities, enabling eavesdroppers to breach the system's guaranteed security. Consequently, developing security models that reflect real-world hardware is essential for assessing actual attack susceptibility. This paper introduces a practical implementation security model for the measurement device in QKD systems, incorporating specific attack scenarios to derive error rates in both quantum bit and key bits as functions of these imperfections. Ultimately, this model offers a framework for assessing the resilience of current commercial QKD hardware against side-channel attacks.

Future mobile networks will rely on Network Function Virtualization (NFV) and Containerization to achieve flexible, efficient resource management. A critical aspect of this domain is forecasting key performance indicators (KPIs) and managing resources effectively. This study proposes a novel Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) deep learning framework designed to predict NFV and containerization behaviors, with a specific focus on container size forecasting. Experiments conducted on live OpenStack cloud infrastructure demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing methods in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the research introduces an enhanced heuristic algorithm optimized for submodular functions, which improves the accuracy of resource forecasting and management. Finally, simulation results confirm the effectiveness of this proposed resource management algorithm.

Concurrently, in 1935, C. Berreth improved upon these works through modifications. However, these generalized frameworks have largely been disregarded in recent decades. The objective of this paper is to rectify that oversight by re-examining these generalized structures using fixed-point theorems recently established in 2014 and semi-metric spaces in 2015 by W.A. Kirk and their co-authors in a generalized form. Let $p$ be a prime number. This work investigates the sequential minimums of specific $\mathbb{Z}_p$-modules within number fields. We establish several distinct $\mathbb{Z}_p$-modules whose sequential minimums exhibit distinct behaviors at $p$. These findings are applied to the analysis of integral generators within ring integers of $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension number fields.

This study utilizes dual-probe enhanced Raman scattering (e-CARS) to measure temperature and concentration in the gas phase, aiming to evaluate the technique's ability to handle multiple simultaneous species. One e-CARS probe employs a bulk anti-stokes crystal for signal enhancement while the other is tuned specifically for methane ($CH_4$), allowing diagnostics even at low concentrations. Experiments were conducted in a two-dimensional $45^\circ$-plate heat pipe, where the probe pair measured the coexistence of nitrogen and methane, capturing both nitrogen temperature profiles and $CH_4$ spatial distributions. Results indicate that this dual-probe setup delivers an improved signal-to-noise ratio and offers higher temporal resolution than single-probe configurations, establishing it as a robust tool for tracing lighter gas species at trace levels. Furthermore, the method successfully monitors natural or forced convective flows of nitrogen carrying natural $CH_4$ plumes, demonstrating its efficacy for observing forced transport mechanisms and the diffusion-driven dispersion of anthropogenic pollutants.

The core accretion model remains the leading explanation for planet formation, positing that dust in protoplanetary disks aggregates over time to create rocky exoplanets. A critical hurdle in this theory is the "final meter problem," which involves the transition from micron-sized particles to pebble-sized bodies; current models have yet to definitively resolve the mechanisms allowing dust to surmount traditional growth obstacles. A promising candidate for overcoming these limits is dust dusting, driven by spatial variations in gas drag that create relative velocities between particles of different sizes. This phenomenon generates low-frequency oscillatory drift patterns capable of inducing collisions. While dusting has successfully been shown to facilitate the growth of pebbles into planetesimals, existing simulations often rely on periodic boundary conditions that fail to capture the full range of flow dynamics. To address this, we conducted three-dimensional, periodic-free, high-resolution, and high-Samaghi simulations of the HD 163296 disk, which exhibits distinct concentric rings due to gaps created by forming planets. Our results reveal that dusting creates a mesh-like, self-organized structure extending across multiple gaps, effectively trapping millimeter- to centimeter-scale particles. Crucially, this trapping mechanism allows the growth of dust beyond gaps to subsequent growth into larger bodies, a process that standard hydrodynamics simulations alone cannot account for.

Quantum Hall edge states typically transport only electrons, rendering neutral modes useless as information carriers. However, in certain out-of-equilibrium circuits, these neutral modes can facilitate the reconstruction of a dc charge current. We demonstrate that applying a dc voltage bias across an out-of-equilibrium Quantum Anomalous Hall (QAH) bar, which hosts a specific neutral chiral edge mode, results in a voltage probe at its center. The origin of this effect lies in the bias-dependent nonequilibrium carrier distribution within the QAH material, which generates a dc charge current terminating at the probe. Notably, this QAH response is amplified by a factor of four compared to standard Quantum Hall setups. The reconstructed current at the probe is robust against variations in the bias contact's geometry and size. Furthermore, the magnitude of this current serves as a direct indicator of the number of neutral edge modes present.

This work introduces a rigid cluster model, which assigns a cluster structure to every cluster variable within the most general cluster-manifold introduced by Fock and Goncharov. We demonstrate that the quantum $A$-side cluster structure of ${\bf u}_q(\mathfrak{g})^*$, when $\mathfrak{g}$ is a simply-laced finite-type Lie algebra, is realized as a Lusitonian dual cluster structure of type $B$ derived from an appropriate dual cluster structure of type $A$ in ${\bf u}_q(\mathfrak{g})$. Furthermore, we construct a ${\bf W}$-invariant $R$-matrix satisfying the hexagon equations relative to the paired ${\bf W}$-invariant cluster structures of types $A$ and $B$ on the dual quantum algebra ${\bf u}_q(\mathfrak{g})$.

This paper introduces a method for robust and decentralized learning that addresses the vulnerabilities of existing approaches to data poisoning attacks. Our approach, known as Distributionally Robust-DSGD (DR-DSGD), operates in a federated environment where multiple clients share a server, learning from potentially contaminated data distributions. To achieve this, the framework formulates a min-max optimization problem that incorporates a robust distribution. A key innovation is the use of an empirical distribution to estimate this robust distribution, which allows the method to function in a fully decentralized manner without requiring communication with a central authority. The convergence of DR-DSGD is proven under both convex and non-convex conditions, demonstrating its superiority over current decentralized and robust learning methods by achieving lower final optimization risks. Furthermore, experiments on image classification tasks confirm that DR-DSGD provides stronger defenses against distributional shifts and data poisoning attacks compared to the state-of-the-art. In terms of architecture, DR-DSGD mirrors Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD) but adds a single additional communication round per training iteration, thereby preserving the high communication efficiency of DSGD and addressing the limitations of more complex, less efficient methods like Fully Homomorphic Encryption or Quantization.

This paper presents a novel, highly efficient algorithm for generating highly accurate, near-canonical hard-disk configurations. We introduce a new event-based Monte Carlo method that combines our most effective local optimization algorithm with an estimator for root-mean-square pressure. Although this pressure estimate is merely a heuristic, it enables rapid convergence of free-energy-based moves, resulting in an algorithm that is both computationally efficient and precise. Consequently, we achieve near-perfect agreement with the virial-based pressure definition across nearly the entire range of interest for the hard-disk system. Furthermore, we derive the exact values for the first six virial coefficients. By integrating these into a new free-energy-based move, we calculate the complete grand canonical ensemble for the hard-disk model. This approach is significantly more efficient than standard methods, requiring only a 1% reduction in sampling time to achieve a 100-fold reduction in statistical error. Additionally, we determine accurate estimates for the activity and compressibility within the first-order transition region. Finally, we determine the exact values for the second and third order derivatives of the pressure with respect to activity within the first-order transition region.

This study employs JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4 to investigate in-medium jet modifications, with a focus on the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$), the lepton charge ratio, and the lepton asymmetry within lepton pairs. Simulations utilize p+Pb collision data at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$ TeV, replicating experimental findings regarding centralities, transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$), and transverse momentum ($p_{\mathrm{T}}$). Our results indicate that central collisions exhibit minimal effects on the lepton charge ratio and lepton charge asymmetry in isolated lepton pairs. Furthermore, the simulated lepton charge distribution aligns closely with the measured lepton charge distribution in the lepton charge.

Our simulated data further demonstrates that the lepton charge distribution aligns closely with the experimentally observed lepton charge distribution in lepton charge.

Pyramid schemes are fraudulent business models that derive revenue for existing participants by enrolling new members and charging them fees; the abstract of the paper discusses how these schemes often utilize deceptive marketing tactics to conceal their true nature, with a specific focus on "MLM," a camouflaged variant that propagates through social media. Leveraging a definition of pyramid scheme constructed from multiple logical arguments, this research identifies their underlying structure by analyzing the content shared among these networks. Furthermore, to detect such schemes, a new methodology utilizing a network constructed via the co-occurrence of joined online communities is proposed. This approach diverges from existing techniques that rely on direct content inspection, instead targeting the network's topological anomalies. Experimental results confirm the approach's efficacy in recognizing these schemes across various datasets.

We have identified 14 potential globular clusters in the inner Galactic bulge, each characterized by a half-light radius of 2.5 pc or more and a half-mass of $10^4 M_{\odot}$ or more, utilizing data from the V-band and near-infrared (JHKs bands) from the HSC-SSI survey. These findings were derived from the spatial distribution analysis of red giant stars within the bulge. By integrating these results with previous findings, we estimate that the variation in reddening ($E(B-V)$) and total-to-selective extinction ratio ($R_V$) across the bulge spans from 0.9 to 3.2 and 3.5 to 6.5, respectively. These ranges represent the distribution of distinct clusters and support the hypothesis that the bulge resides within multiple gravitational potential wells. Furthermore, the coexistence of these candidate clusters and the observed diversity in $R_V$ values suggest that the bulge contains a population of young globular clusters.

We present a practical computational framework for such spectra by integrating them within the FELA system, which utilizes the FELA_DY system for DY calculations. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through a detailed analysis of the fully differential $p p \to \ell^+ \ell^- X$ reaction at the LHC, specifically focusing on transverse lepton momentum and rapidity distributions. This study examines the application of tight-binding models within light-matter interactions, specifically contrasting the velocity and dipole gauges. While the velocity gauge is traditionally favored for its simplicity, it often encounters difficulties representing phenomena tied to the electric dipole approximation. We demonstrate that the dipole gauge offers a more straightforward description of such phenomena, provided that the corresponding vector potential remains expressed in a specific gauge-transformed form. Furthermore, we derive a general mapping between the velocity and dipole gauges that preserves the physical equivalence of the resulting tight-binding models. Finally, we apply these methodologies to derive an octupole-corrected tight-binding model suitable for describing light-matter interaction in inversion-symmetric materials like graphene.

We introduce a family of highly symmetric, contractible, and highly degenerate, yet correctable, holographic tensor networks. These structures exhibit pronounced symmetry, degeneracy, and quantum error correction capabilities. By implementing a diagonal Petz map, we demonstrate that these networks facilitate highly symmetric quantum error correction. Consequently, a substantial portion of the recovered state's degeneracy remains structured and symmetric. Specifically, we find that a highly symmetric subset can be restored with even greater symmetry within the remaining degenerate subspace.

A two-state, two-mode computational model was employed to investigate the transient dynamics and steady-state quantum yields within a photoisomerization reaction. By fitting model parameters to experimental femtosecond pump-probe data, we demonstrated that the two-level framework accurately captures the reaction's transient behaviors. Furthermore, a distinct sensitivity contrast was observed: both the steady-state yield and the characteristic isomerization timescale exhibited high sensitivity to system parameters under transient conditions, whereas steady-state quantum yield remained largely insensitive to these variations when retinal initial population was low. This contrast highlights a decoupling between dynamic and stationary outcomes, highlighting how the chromophore's initial state can dictate final stationary results independent of specific retinal vs. ionized pathways.

Process-mining relies on the application of various neural network architectures, including Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), with studies suggesting RNNs often yield the most effective outcomes. To evaluate these approaches, this paper introduces a benchmark using twelve real-world, labeled datasets. We conducted experiments with carefully configured baseline models for each network architecture to ensure a fair comparison. Additionally, we tested various RNN models and auxiliary strategies, such as different attention mechanisms and pre-trained word embeddings. The results offered by this study provide a crucial foundation for future process-mining research.

Social media plays a dual role in both disaster management and public relations, serving as a tool for disseminating crucial information and for gauging public sentiment. In this study, we utilize Twitter data to analyze sentiment regarding earthquakes. We employ the VADER library for automated sentiment analysis and apply the Weibo- based approach to extract emotional trends. Our results demonstrate that this framework is highly effective for monitoring public emotions concerning seismic events via social media platforms.

Assessing the potential for life-supporting atmospheres on exoplanets requires evaluating the impact of high-energy radiation from their host stars. While much research has focused on X-rays and ultraviolet (UV) output, this study examines the effects of stellar flares across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, with a specific emphasis on ionizing flux generated by flare-generated X-ray/UV emission and the flux of energetic particles such as protons and electrons. Using white-light flare distributions derived from Kepler data for solar-type stars, we calculate atmospheric erosion driven by energy-limited hydrodynamic escape under varying stellar activity levels, atmospheric compositions, and atmospheric masses. Our results indicate that for exoplanets orbiting Sun-like stars, flares are the primary driver of atmospheric escape, surpassing the effects of quiescent X-ray/UV emission. This finding is especially significant for planets with low-mass atmospheres, such as those potentially harboring biosignatures. Consequently, accurate analysis of exospheres, remote sensing of atmospheres, and the identification of biosignatures must incorporate the influence of flares-induced erosion and the flux of energetic particles.

This study introduces a periodic waveguide network, consisting of two parallel waveguide arrays periodically interconnected by connecting channels. We establish the conditions required to achieve bi-directional reflectionless transmission within such a structure. Specifically, this outcome is realized when the interconnection period is an integer multiple of the spatially coupled lattice's bi-directional transmission period. By integrating a transfer matrix method with a tight-binding model, this research elucidates the underlying physics governing bi-directional reflectionless transmission and demonstrates the ability to position unidirectional reflectionless states arbitrarily within the system. Furthermore, the design of a three-dimensional photonic circuit capable of achieving bi-directional reflectionless transmission over a broad frequency range and confining unidirectional reflectionless transmission at specific frequencies is illustrated through a practical application.

We present a probabilistic framework designed to infer the dynamic structure of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from time-series expression data. This approach explicitly models biological noise, accounting for both random fluctuations in single-cell data and variability arising from averaging across populations. We establish theoretical results demonstrating the framework's dynamic structural consistency under specific conditions. Complementing this, a computationally efficient variational algorithm is introduced to estimate the model parameters and network interactions from biological replicates. The method is validated through simulations and experimental data, with a key finding being the critical importance of bidirectionality in gene regulation. The following sections detail the proposed probabilistic model, theoretical guarantees, estimation algorithms, and empirical performance comparisons.

Present novel compact formulae for the basis transformation coefficients linking single-particle bases, as well as formulae for one- and two-body physical operators. These formulae have been implemented in `nxt`, an open-source application designed to handle nuclear many-body operator and basis transformation calculations alongside various single- and multi-particle properties. The formulae for basis transformation coefficients and one-body operators enable the efficient computation of basis-transformed two-body matrix elements, nuclear energy levels, and nuclear masses. Additionally, the new formulae for two-body matrix elements facilitate the development of efficient code implementing particle-hole, quasi-particle, and other transformations built upon these data.

Neural network architectures utilizing point clouds have demonstrated remarkable success in tasks such as semantic segmentation, labeling, and classification. Nevertheless, the majority of these models remain vulnerable to adversarial examples. This study presents the first comprehensive analysis of adversarial attacks on point cloud classification and semantic segmentation. Our research reveals that current point cloud models achieve lower accuracy and F1-scores under adversarial conditions compared to their counterparts in images and 2D point sets. Furthermore, we identify and categorize three common types of 3D transformations—permutation, scaling, and rigid body motions—while conducting attack strategies specific to each type. Additionally, we introduce a novel "Copy-Paste" attack designed to target point clouds with out-of-distribution transformations. Surprisingly, our method yields the most effective results against standard augmentation techniques, causing complete segmentation failure across all tested architectures. In contrast, our investigation into white-box and black-box recovery attacks shows that successful perturbation addition is feasible with lower required query counts or gradient access. Lastly, we suggest a black-box counter-attack to mitigate the efficacy of the Copy-Paste strategy. All experimental code and pre-generated adversarial examples are made publicly available.

This study examines medium access control (MAC) protocols specifically designed for FMCW radar networks operating under CSMA/CCA mechanisms. In this framework, each node utilizes its own protocol parameters to create distinct access patterns, allowing for the construction of cooperative schemes where nodes assist one another. Decisions regarding transmission or reception are driven by the Clear Channel Assessment (CCA), which relies on the presence of interference at a receiver to determine channel occupancy status. The paper formulates the performance evaluation of these radar protocols as a continuous-time Markov process, presenting the general mathematical structures for both received signal rates and effective data rates. Furthermore, specific analytical models are developed for two scenarios: a basic non-cooperative framework and a multi-hop relay-assisted system. Performance metrics are derived based on various initial conditions, with practical numerical results validated through comparisons against Monte-Carlo simulations.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (TKGC) has emerged as a popular technique for reasoning about event and temporal data graphs, specifically aiming to infer missing information by leveraging available entries. Within this field, Tensor Factorization (TF) methods are widely adopted for constructing logical representations of time-dependent relationships and entities. Nevertheless, traditional MF, BPR, and their variants rely heavily on manually designed distance functions and ranking objectives, which often fail to capture the nuanced patterns hidden within complex temporal interactions. To address this shortcoming, this study introduces AutoTLM, an innovative framework that replaces these fixed components with trainable auto-taloe representations. By integrating BERT-based language pre-training with automatic taloring mechanisms, AutoTLM adapts to specific graph structures and user preferences, thereby enhancing the expressiveness of representation learning for TKGs. Furthermore, the proposed work incorporates BPR with self-loops to refine the loss function through iterative feedback loops. Comprehensive assessments across two diverse datasets demonstrate that AutoTLM substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of accuracy and robustness.

The Jost function method has been employed to analyze the Jost parameters within the complex momentum plane for electric dipole $1^{-}$ states in $^{16}$O. This approach yields precise root locations in the complex momentum plane, from which the complex energies of electric dipole $1^{-}$ excitations are derived. The resulting Jost parameter results align closely with those obtained from a complex optical potential. Our findings indicate that the dominant giant resonance in the electric dipole sector consists of two poles: one broad pole corresponding to the well-known $1^{-}$ giant dipole resonance, and another pole situated on the unphysical sheet far from the energy axis, which is associated with a narrow state. The origin and physical significance of this narrow pole remain unclear and warrant further investigation.

Most clustering applications analyze a system at a single snapshot, overlooking its dynamic evolution. However, this paper considers applying clustering dynamics to dynamic systems. To achieve this, we introduce Dynamic System Clustering Dynamics (DSCD). The proposed method integrates the standard system dynamics approach with the push-sum structure. Specifically, the vector field is partitioned into distinct regions (basins), and the initial conditions within each region are assigned to corresponding stable states. Numerical results demonstrate that the new approach is capable of classifying complex data, such as the Drosophila embryo segmentation problem. In addition, the method is able to reconstruct the data of the Swiss Reiter attractor more accurately than the existing standard system dynamics approach.

Implementing neural text generation models via Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) presents significant challenges due to the non-differentiability of the full training loop, a limitation that has hindered their success in text generation compared to other modalities. To address this, we introduce CycleTextGAN, a framework built on the principles of cyclic consistency and discriminators operating at multiple levels. Our method ensures complete differentiability throughout the training process by leveraging a hierarchical structure that decomposes sentences into constituent words and clauses. By generating these smaller linguistic units independently and recombining them to construct cyclic-consistent cyclegraphs, CycleTextGAN achieves robust generation across diverse language tasks. Empirical results indicate that our approach surpasses leading state-of-the-art techniques in various evaluation metrics.

The concept that life could migrate between planets via asteroids and comets, known as **interstellar panspermia**, has long been considered theoretically feasible. While the mechanism itself is straightforward to model, validating it through observations is difficult due to the vast range of timescales and spatial scales involved. To overcome this, we propose a novel approach utilizing the **Galactic magnetic field** as a "cosmic ruler." By combining observations of the **Larmor radii** of cosmic rays with data on their anisotropy, we can determine the typical Larmor radius scale in space. Applying this to interstellar panspermia, we can estimate the characteristic size of interstellar asteroids and comets ($\sim$100 m) and their spatial clustering scale ($\sim$1000 AU). These estimates, in turn, allow us to calculate the characteristic migration timescale for life, which we estimate to be roughly $10^6$ years ($1$ million years). Consequently, life could potentially traverse an average distance of $10$ light-years ($1$ light-year) within a single migration cycle, visiting numerous star systems across the Milky Way. This unique model predicts that if interstellar panspermia is active, the **biological signatures** (biosignatures) present in planetary atmospheres should exhibit specific spatial correlations in their **graininess** (granularity) caused by the combined effects of Larmor diffusion and clustering. This work investigates a spontaneous symmetry breaking mechanism applicable to all four Standard Model gauge interactions, proposing that the Higgs boson is actually a composite state formed from bound constituents. This new "composite mechanism" relies on the concept of asymptotic freedom within the $SU(4)_L \times U(1)_{Y}$ extension of the Standard Model. In this framework, fermion resonances emerge as elementary counterparts to elementary fermions found in the Standard Model. Furthermore, it establishes a direct connection between the mass of the discovered Higgs boson and the mass spectrum of these new fermionic resonances.

In wildlife research, resource selection functions (RSFs) are frequently utilized to analyze spatial animal movement and resource selection patterns by processing location data alongside environmental covariates. A key strength of RSFs is their flexibility in modeling complex, non-linear relationships between covariates through various algorithmic approaches, including generalized additive models (GAMs), random forests, and gradient boosting. However, a gap exists in the literature regarding the development of confidence intervals for RSF covariate estimates. We propose a nonparametric bootstrap approach designed to generate confidence intervals for these estimates. Through a gradient boosting-based RSF model applied to the GPS-tracked GPSMove dataset of collared mountain lions in Colorado, we demonstrate the suggested interval method. Furthermore, comparisons with a standard bootstrap variant reveal that the new method achieves superior coverage performance.

Given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with edge lengths $l(e)$ for each $e \in E$, the minimum power network design problem seeks to assign a non-negative power value $p(v)$ to every node $v \in V$ such that every node $u$ can reach nodes powered by at least $\min\{d(u,v), l(e)\}$ for all edges $e$ incident to $u$. This problem is NP-hard and has previously been addressed by a $2$-approximation algorithm. We improve upon this by presenting an $\frac{11}{6}$-approximation algorithm, which is further enhanced to $\frac{11}{6}$ for graphs where every edge length is either $1$ or $2$. Additionally, for graphs restricted to edge lengths of $1$ and $2$, we introduce an asymptotically tight $\frac{11}{6}$-approximation.

This study outlines a methodology for autonomously planning and executing missions for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to support human search and rescue (SAR) operations. In this framework, a command center designates a specific target area where at least one survivor is presumed present, while the UAVs, operating with only partially known environments, search for them. Once a rescue is confirmed, the system immediately directs the UAVs to transport life-saving supplies directly to the survivors. To achieve this, an $A^*$ pathfinding algorithm is employed to route the aircraft toward the mission objective. Furthermore, a novel communication model is introduced to account for realistic signal constraints, specifically defining a "silent zone" within which autonomous decision-making is mandatory due to communication blackouts. Furthermore, this paper presents the logic behind a human-machine interface (HMI) built using JavaFX, which manages the execution of these UAV operations.

Localization of dynamics on networks is governed by nodal activity and is influenced by network topology, a connection that remains insufficiently understood. This study reveals a mechanism for self-organized localization by examining how dynamical drivers interact with driver-free network nodes. We demonstrate that when driving forces are tuned to match the natural frequencies of highly active (no-node) regions, self-localization occurs. Conversely, driving at the resonant frequencies of low-activity nodes results in dynamics that favor those same nodes, thereby amplifying their inherent activation. These findings indicate that low driving amplitudes, when aligned with nodal intrinsic properties, can trigger localized dynamics. Such insights are applicable to diverse contexts, ranging from biological systems to technological infrastructures.

Evaluating team and individual performance in football is a critical research focus, with defense often proving more complex to assess than offense. While previous studies often evaluate defense solely by goals conceded, this paper argues that defense must also account for the quality of opposition attacks and whether a team was playing away or home. To this end, we analyze the English Premier League (EPL) from the 2016/17 to the 2019/20 seasons using a Poisson regression model to calculate a new defensive metric: Total Defense Strength (TDS). Our findings indicate that 67% of the variance in goals conceded is explained by the average attacking strength faced and whether games were played away, leaving only 33% for factors specific to a team's defense. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating TDS into a betting strategy significantly outperforms models relying exclusively on average attacking and defensive statistics.

Extracting information from form image templates is a challenging natural image processing issue, particularly when dealing with historical versions that suffer from degraded ink quality, damaged paper, and ambiguous labeling. Existing deep learning-driven solutions often require extensive manual annotation and often fail to account for the structural layout of a form. This study introduces a cost-sensitive deep learning template that leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to detect and classify input fields. The proposed approach utilizes a multi-task learning architecture that integrates both a content-based module and a layout module. The layout component employs a CNN to predict a spatial representation of a form's layout, while the content component maps specific image regions to corresponding textual labels. The proposed method is evaluated on a newly compiled dataset of 1,500 image templates sourced from various government agencies, including postal services, banks, and tax authorities. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a 94.2% detection rate and a 95.6% classification accuracy. The source code is available at https://github.com/rahmanimam/Form-Detection-and-Classification.

Hidden-Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HP-RSSMs) represent a recent advancement over standard Reversible Susspace Movement Models (RSSMs) by introducing latent noise parameters that are only identifiable within specific noise contexts. These models are theoretically grounded in the capability to learn distinct system dynamics under varying noise conditions. However, current research has been confined to the analysis of simulated environments, leaving an open question regarding their efficacy with actual real-world time series. This study addresses HP-RSSMs across a diverse spectrum of physical systems, including data from pendulums, robotic arms, human and animal locomotion, and molecular vibrations. We present new data-derived datasets, some of which are publicly accessible, and establish baseline performance metrics for HP-RSSMs. Furthermore, we conducted a comparative analysis against standard RSSMs and other leading models, revealing that HP-RSSMs are particularly adept at modeling systems exhibiting dynamic shifts in noise characteristics.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit asymptotic freeness as $N$ approaches infinity, a property that implies the non-commutative independence of unitarily invariant and Haar unitary matrices. This paper explores the concept of a "near" version of such freeness within the unitary conjugate class, defined by $\mathcal{M}_N = \{ UAU^* \mid U \in \mathfrak{U}_N\}$, where $A$ is a Hermitian matrix with a bounded, non-random empirical spectral distribution $\mu_A$. We demonstrate that the convergence of moments occurs at a rate of $O(N^{-2})$ for pairs of such unitary conjugate sets. Furthermore, we analyze the joint distribution of $k$ Haar unitary matrices $U_1, \dots, U_k$ acting on a deterministic Hermitian matrix $A$ via conjugation, tracing trajectories on the Stieltmann hierarchy of partitions for trace invariants. These paths are determined by the specific spectral measure $\mu_A$, with the trajectories themselves depending on the conjugation action.

In fields where the characteristic is not 2, consider a non-superelliptic, geometrically integral smooth curve $C$ within a complete, smooth toric surface $S$ defined over $\mathbb{R}$ such that $S(\mathbb{R})$ is connected. If the Jacobian $J(C)$ admits an abelian variety $A$ with abelian multiplicity $m \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ satisfying $J(C) \sim_m A$, then there exists a finite morphism $\pi: C' \to C$ of degree $k!$ for some integer $k \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that $J(C') \sim A$. Furthermore, the surface $S$ is defined by $\mathbb{R}$-rational coordinates, and the transformed curve $C'$ shares these properties as a non-superelliptic, geometrically integral smooth, entirely rationalized toric surface $S$ of degree $k!$ in the same surface $S$ where $J(C') \sim A$.

This paper evaluates ten polarization measurement methods across five distinct social networks, normalizing all scores to facilitate performance comparison. We analyze the effects of normalization, data volume, and measurement frequency by varying these parameters independently. Results indicate that normalization significantly alters scores and can either amplify or diminish the relative performance of specific methods. Furthermore, certain methods demonstrated improved accuracy as network size increased, whereas others maintained consistent performance regardless of scale. Finally, our analysis reveals that two methods achieved superior accuracy with higher measurement frequencies, whereas increasing frequency for remaining methods did not necessarily enhance their scores.

Multilayer networks offer a superior framework for modeling the dynamics of complex, interconnected systems compared to single-layer models. Although their descriptive power is evident, the computational challenges of simulating dynamics on such structures remain significant. This study introduces a set of techniques designed to sparsify the adjacency matrices used in multilayer network models, enabling efficient simulation without altering the underlying dynamics. We validate our approach by demonstrating that sparse approximations yield dynamical trajectories nearly indistinguishable from those of the dense originals, while drastically reducing memory requirements and computational time. Our findings reveal that these methods are especially effective for systems exhibiting synchronous behavior or those constrained to low-dimensional dynamical manifolds, resulting in substantial sparsification. Ultimately, this research supplies a practical means to simulate large-scale multilayer systems with both high performance and accuracy.

When analyzing the balance of linear momentum in continuum mechanics, it can be expressed as $-div \, \sigma = f$, where $\sigma$ denotes the Cauchy stress operator and $f$ represents the density of body forces. Within the framework of mechanics, this differential expression is typically treated as a constraint; however, in contemporary artificial life models involving continuous media, $div \, \sigma = f$ is often utilized directly as an evolutionary PDE for $\sigma$. This paper investigates such interpretation by examining differential properties of $div \, \sigma = f$ when $div \, \sigma$ functions as a differential operator. We establish the existence of a specific adjoint stress operator, termed the *adjoint Cauchy stress*, defined as $W=\text{adj}\, div$. This operator satisfies $div \, \sigma = f = W Z$ for some $Z$. Notably, $W$ exhibits properties analogous to the Piola–Kirchhoff stress operator found in classical continuum mechanics. Additionally, we introduce a discrete counterpart to $W$ within a discrete setting derived from a space-discretized formulation of $div \, \sigma = f$.

Formal verification techniques are increasingly being adopted to detect and mitigate software bugs, with a specific focus on enhancing the reliability of safety-critical systems. This essay explores both the theoretical foundations and practical applications of testing and verification within general programming, with testing highlighted as a ubiquitous method for uncovering defects. It examines the connections between formal verification and software testing, analyzing how they complement one another. Furthermore, the discussion highlights several cutting-edge approaches to generating test cases that verify specific properties, alongside an overview of logical frameworks employed to establish the correctness of algorithms and system designs.

Prompt Tuning has recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for parameter-efficient transfer learning, yet it still requires freezing pre-trained model weights and introducing task-specific auxiliary layers. To further streamline the process of aligning features for task adaptation, we introduce HyperPrompt, a prompt-tuning strategy utilizing shared hyper-prompts to create task-independent feature mappings. These HyperPrompts are designed to inject task-invariant information into model layers, facilitating the alignment of base model representations with task-targeted task-adaptation. Experiments demonstrate that HyperPrompts facilitate superior performance across multiple downstream tasks compared to static prompt variants and fine-tuning baselines. Surprisingly, these benefits are achieved with an extremely low training complexity, as indicated by a learning curve analysis.

Let $\Phi$ be a root system of type $A_n$ with $n \geq 3$, and $K$ be a field with characteristic not equal to $2$. The authors demonstrate that the orbits of $SO(\alpha|_{\mathfrak{B}})$ acting on the set of generic configurations of $\alpha$-orthogonal roots in the standard representation of $B(\alpha)$ (the Bondal algebra of $\alpha$) are in correspondence with the orbits of $SO(\alpha)$ acting on $\alpha$. Specifically, there exists an orbit-preserving, explicit construction of a morphism from $\beta=\otimes_{\Phi} G(\alpha)$ to $G(\alpha)$, where $\beta$ denotes the subset of $\beta \in \beta$ such that $\beta = \beta/2$.

This study introduces a new class of non-classical quantum states, termed parity-symmetry-enforced-photon-emissions-restricted-quantum-states, defined by the requirement that photon emissions up to a specific moment in a quantum system's evolution are prohibited by parity symmetry. These states facilitate the generation of photon emissions with a predetermined temporal pattern upon breaching symmetry-imposed blockade conditions. Our analysis reveals that breaching symmetry-constrained conditions produces correlated quantum jumps characterized by an extended timescale relative to standard free-evolution dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these states support Markovian feedback operations capable of accelerating standard quantum-by-way-coding. Lastly, we illustrate practical applications within the context of superconducting artificial atoms operating under parity restrictions.

This study addresses the challenge of constructing a resilient, fully decentralized, and self-organizing network in the presence of malicious actors. We introduce a self-stabilizing, self-configuration algorithm for a permissionless, anonymous, and lock-free system where nodes communicate via reliable point-to-point links. In this framework, only a constant fraction of nodes are Byzantine, while the remainder are crash-prone but anonymous; crucially, no node possesses prior knowledge of the total population size or the specific count of Byzantine actors. Upon execution, this algorithm enables the construction of a correct, fault-tolerant network among the honest nodes. This resulting network is self-healing, meaning that even if the initial configuration is incorrect or an external agent introduces data corruption, the algorithm ensures that every reliable node eventually establishes the network correctly. Furthermore, the protocol guarantees that every honest participant will ultimately become aware of the identity of every malicious node, regardless of whether they have initial knowledge of the total population size. In terms of communication complexity, the algorithm requires $O(n^2)$ messages per node to achieve convergence. Finally, the study examines the scenario where nodes are not anonymous, demonstrating that if each node knows its own identity and that of others, the algorithm can be adapted to also allow the total population size to be known by all nodes, while still permitting a larger proportion of Byzantine actors relative to the anonymous setting.

This research introduces a nonparametric methodology for estimating traffic signal timing parameters by analyzing probe vehicle trajectory and timing information. The approach conditions signal states on specific events, such as vehicle arrivals or departures, and employs conditional queue length data to determine timing settings. Leveraging high-frequency vehicle counts from the ETC lane on expressways as a proxy, the method utilizes a Negative Binomial distribution to model these queue lengths and optimizes signal timing via maximum likelihood estimation. Validation through a case study utilizing real-world FMC (Frequency Modulated Communication) dataset confirms the technique's efficacy.

Numerical relativity simulations in dynamical spacetimes require solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints alongside evolution equations. While methods for handling constraint satisfaction have been extensively developed for vacuum scenarios, effective solutions for treating matter are far less advanced. In this study, we propose a novel, straightforward algorithm to resolve the Hamiltonian constraint by treating it as a differential equation. We implemented this method within the Spacetime Algebra (SA) framework, utilizing an approach to SA that naturally accommodates numerical relativity. Specifically, we employed a formulation where multivector fields depend on spacetime coordinates, utilizing a tetrads-based metric formulation. Within this framework, both Einstein's equations and standard matter equations translate into simple differential equations for scalar, vector, and bivector components. We tested this method against a numerical generation involving a Schwarzschild spacetime distorted by numerical noise and compared our approach to the traditional Gauss-Seidel technique. Results indicate that our algorithm converges more rapidly and yields a more accurate solution to the Hamiltonian constraint. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of this method within a dynamical context by solving Einstein-Klein-Gordon equations for spacetimes containing holes in a scalar field. We observed that this algorithm efficiently propagates constraint violations through spacetime, a behavior essential for other numerical relativity applications.
